questions.learning_objective: Prioritize synchronized cardioversion for wide-complex tachycardia with a pulse and cardiopulmonary compromise.
questions.stem: A 13-year-old hospitalized with myocarditis develops a regular wide-complex tachycardia. He has a pulse but is hypotensive, confused, and poorly perfused. What is the most appropriate immediate rhythm treatment?

options.text: Urgent synchronized cardioversion while resuscitation and expert support continue
Observation because ventricular tachycardia is often transient in myocarditis
Give adenosine first regardless of rhythm regularity or hemodynamic compromise
Start an oral beta-blocker and reassess later
Obtain CMR before treating the rhythm

questions.rationale: Wide-complex tachycardia with a pulse plus hypotension, altered mental status, or shock is an unstable tachyarrhythmia. Pediatric advanced life support prioritizes synchronized cardioversion rather than delayed pharmacologic or diagnostic maneuvers.

option_explanations.sync_cardio: Correct. Cardiopulmonary compromise changes the priority from rhythm diagnosis refinement to immediate electrical stabilization.
option_explanations.observe: Nonsustained asymptomatic ectopy may sometimes be monitored, but sustained wide-complex tachycardia with shock is immediately dangerous.
option_explanations.adenosine_any: Adenosine can have a diagnostic/therapeutic role in selected regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia without compromise, but unstable patients need synchronized cardioversion. Irregular wide-complex rhythms are particularly unsafe for indiscriminate adenosine use.
option_explanations.oral_beta: Oral therapy is too slow for an unstable rhythm and may worsen hemodynamics depending on the context.
option_explanations.wait_cmr: Imaging must not delay treatment of a life-threatening arrhythmia.

questions.board_pearl: In pediatric wide-complex tachycardia, hemodynamic stability determines urgency: compromise means synchronized cardioversion.

evidence.claim: Pediatric wide-complex tachycardia with cardiopulmonary compromise should be treated with synchronized cardioversion.

questions.learning_objective: Prioritize defibrillation and high-quality CPR when myocarditis deteriorates to a shockable cardiac-arrest rhythm.
questions.stem: A 10-year-old with fulminant myocarditis suddenly becomes unresponsive and pulseless. The monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the immediate priority?

options.text: Rapid defibrillation with high-quality CPR according to pediatric cardiac-arrest care
Give an antiarrhythmic medication before the first shock
Perform a complete echocardiogram before starting CPR
Confirm myocarditis by biopsy before treating the arrest
Use synchronized cardioversion because all ventricular rhythms should be synchronized

questions.rationale: VF and pulseless VT are shockable pediatric cardiac-arrest rhythms. Rapid defibrillation and high-quality CPR are the priority; myocarditis is the underlying cause, not a reason to delay standard resuscitation.

option_explanations.defib_cpr: Correct. Defibrillation is the definitive immediate treatment for VF/pulseless VT, with high-quality CPR minimizing no-flow time.
option_explanations.amio_first: Antiarrhythmics can be used in refractory shockable arrest, but they do not replace the priority of early defibrillation and CPR.
option_explanations.echo_first: Point-of-care echo may help identify reversible causes during arrest if it does not interrupt compressions, but it must not delay CPR or defibrillation.
option_explanations.biopsy_first: Etiologic confirmation has no role before treating cardiac arrest.
option_explanations.sync_cardio: Synchronized cardioversion is used for unstable tachycardia with a pulse. VF/pulseless VT requires unsynchronized defibrillation.

questions.board_pearl: Myocarditis changes the cause of arrest—not the first priorities of treating VF/pulseless VT.

evidence.claim: Rapid defibrillation is the priority for pediatric cardiac arrest with VF/pulseless VT.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize symptomatic complete heart block in myocarditis as a critical conduction complication requiring ICU management and possible pacing.
questions.stem: An 8-year-old with myocarditis develops complete AV block with dizziness, hypotension, and poor perfusion despite correction of hypoxia and other reversible contributors. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat as symptomatic bradycardia/conduction failure with immediate resuscitation support, ICU escalation, and consideration of emergency pacing
Observe because complete heart block is a benign expected stage of myocarditis
Use light exercise to raise the ventricular rate
Discharge if troponin is falling
Delay treatment until CMR confirms conduction-system inflammation

questions.rationale: High-grade AV block with cardiopulmonary compromise is an emergency. Pediatric resuscitation guidance supports bradycardia management and allows emergency transcutaneous pacing for complete heart block unresponsive to initial resuscitative measures.

option_explanations.brady_escalate: Correct. The key is the combination of conduction block and poor perfusion, not the myocarditis label alone.
option_explanations.benign_block: AV block can be transient in myocarditis, but symptomatic complete block can progress to arrest and is not safe for observation without active management.
option_explanations.sports: Exercise is contraindicated during active myocarditis and cannot safely substitute for pacing or resuscitative care.
option_explanations.discharge: A falling injury marker does not eliminate immediate conduction risk. Disposition is driven by rhythm and perfusion.
option_explanations.cmr_wait: Imaging can clarify inflammation but cannot delay management of symptomatic bradycardia.

questions.board_pearl: In myocarditis, complete AV block plus poor perfusion is a bradycardia emergency, not merely a diagnostic clue.

evidence.claim: Pediatric myocarditis with heart block is a high-risk pre-arrest condition requiring ICU monitoring and therapy.
Emergency pacing may be considered for complete heart block with cardiopulmonary compromise unresponsive to initial resuscitation.

questions.learning_objective: Treat documented NSVT in active myocarditis as meaningful electrical instability even if the child is asymptomatic during the run.
questions.stem: A 7-year-old with myocarditis has a brief run of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia on telemetry but denies symptoms. Ventricular function is mildly depressed. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: It is evidence of electrical instability and supports continued monitored care and risk assessment
It can be ignored because there was no syncope
It is compatible with immediate sports clearance because it was nonsustained
All nonsustained ventricular tachycardia in children should be assumed to be artifact
It proves isolated pericarditis rather than myocardial disease

questions.rationale: Ventricular tachyarrhythmia is clinically significant in myocarditis even without symptoms and is associated with greater morbidity/resource use. The finding changes monitoring and follow-up risk assessment.

option_explanations.electrical_instability: Correct. Absence of symptoms during a short run does not make ventricular tachycardia benign in an inflamed myocardium.
option_explanations.ignore: Syncope would increase concern further, but asymptomatic VT still represents an important electrical complication.
option_explanations.sports: Documented ventricular arrhythmia during active or recovering myocarditis argues against routine clearance until adequately reassessed.
option_explanations.artifact_assume: Telemetry artifact is possible and strips should be reviewed, but true documented NSVT cannot be dismissed categorically.
option_explanations.pericarditis_only: Ventricular tachycardia points to myocardial electrical involvement, not isolated pericardial inflammation.

questions.board_pearl: Asymptomatic ventricular tachycardia is still ventricular tachycardia; symptoms do not define electrical risk.

evidence.claim: Arrhythmias in pediatric myocarditis are associated with worse outcomes and greater resource utilization.
Ventricular arrhythmia is a high-risk feature in pediatric myocarditis.

questions.learning_objective: Pursue intermittent rhythm evaluation when syncope occurs despite a normal resting ECG in myocarditis.
questions.stem: An 11-year-old with suspected myocarditis has an episode of syncope. A resting ECG obtained afterward is unchanged from admission. Which next evaluation most directly addresses a dangerous intermittent cause?

options.text: Review continuous telemetry and obtain appropriate ambulatory/prolonged rhythm monitoring if needed
Assume vasovagal syncope because the post-event ECG is unchanged
Repeat chest radiography as the primary syncope test
Stop cardiac monitoring because the ECG is normal between events
Perform immediate maximal exercise testing during active myocarditis

questions.rationale: Intermittent tachy- or bradyarrhythmias may not appear on a resting ECG. Syncope in myocarditis is a high-risk symptom and warrants rhythm-focused evaluation and continued monitoring.

option_explanations.rhythm_monitor: Correct. Continuous or prolonged monitoring is designed to capture transient electrical events missed by a snapshot ECG.
option_explanations.assume_vagal: Vasovagal syncope is common, but known/suspected myocarditis raises pretest concern for arrhythmia. A benign label should follow, not precede, adequate cardiac assessment.
option_explanations.repeat_cxr: Radiography may evaluate congestion but does not diagnose intermittent arrhythmia.
option_explanations.stop_monitor: A normal between-event ECG does not guarantee electrical stability.
option_explanations.exercise_now: Exercise testing can be valuable later in recovery but is inappropriate as an acute provocation test during active myocarditis.

questions.board_pearl: Syncope plus myocarditis is an intermittent-arrhythmia problem until an adequate rhythm evaluation says otherwise.

evidence.claim: Arrhythmic presentations including syncope are recognized myocarditis phenotypes and require risk stratification.
Myocarditis with arrhythmia or heart block warrants early ICU monitoring and therapy.

questions.learning_objective: Seek expert consultation before antiarrhythmic drug therapy for pediatric wide-complex tachycardia without cardiopulmonary compromise.
questions.stem: A 6-year-old with myocarditis has a regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia but remains alert, normotensive, and well perfused. Which general next-step principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Obtain expert consultation and define the rhythm before choosing antiarrhythmic therapy; selected regular monomorphic rhythms may allow diagnostic/therapeutic adenosine under appropriate monitoring
Immediately perform synchronized cardioversion in every wide-complex rhythm even without cardiopulmonary compromise
Give multiple antiarrhythmic drugs sequentially without specialist input
Use adenosine for any wide-complex tachycardia, including irregular rhythms
Ignore the rhythm because blood pressure is currently normal

questions.rationale: Stable pediatric wide-complex tachycardia has several possible mechanisms, and antiarrhythmic therapy can be proarrhythmic. Current pediatric guidance prioritizes expert consultation; adenosine may be useful only in selected regular monomorphic rhythms.

option_explanations.expert_stable_wct: Correct. Stability creates time for rhythm clarification and expert-guided therapy while the child remains closely monitored.
option_explanations.sync_all: Cardioversion is clearly indicated when cardiopulmonary compromise is present. In a stable child, expert rhythm assessment can guide a less reflexive approach.
option_explanations.drug_stack: Multiple antiarrhythmics can increase proarrhythmic and hemodynamic risk, especially in cardiomyopathy. Specialist-guided selection is preferred.
option_explanations.adenosine_irregular: Adenosine should not be used indiscriminately in irregular wide-complex tachycardia because dangerous pre-excited rhythms are possible. Its role is limited to selected regular monomorphic cases.
option_explanations.ignore: Normal blood pressure does not make WCT benign; continued monitoring and expert evaluation are required.

questions.board_pearl: Stable wide-complex tachycardia buys time for expert rhythm definition—not permission to ignore it or stack drugs.

evidence.claim: For pediatric wide-complex tachycardia without cardiopulmonary compromise, expert consultation is recommended before antiarrhythmic agents; adenosine may be useful when the rhythm is regular and monomorphic.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize that normalization of EF does not erase residual electrical risk.
questions.stem: A 15-year-old recovering from myocarditis has normal LV ejection fraction but frequent ventricular ectopy on ambulatory monitoring. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Mechanical recovery and electrical recovery are distinct; the ectopy requires continued cardiology assessment
Normal EF proves complete cardiac recovery and makes the ectopy irrelevant
The ectopy matters only if troponin is still elevated
Frequent ventricular ectopy is automatically a benign athletic finding in adolescents
Ambulatory monitoring should be stopped once echocardiography normalizes

questions.rationale: Myocarditis recovery is multidimensional. Ventricular function can normalize while scar or electrical instability persists, so rhythm findings remain clinically relevant.

option_explanations.rhythm_independent: Correct. Function, symptoms, biomarkers, tissue findings, and rhythm do not necessarily recover at the same pace.
option_explanations.ef_cures: EF is an important recovery measure but does not capture arrhythmia substrate or active tissue injury.
option_explanations.troponin_only: Troponin may normalize even when electrical risk remains. Rhythm findings should be interpreted directly rather than conditionally on a biomarker.
option_explanations.athlete_normal: Some ectopy can be benign, but frequent or complex ventricular ectopy after myocarditis requires disease-specific assessment before it is labeled physiologic.
option_explanations.no_monitor: Rhythm monitoring is specifically useful in myocarditis follow-up when arrhythmic risk persists.

questions.board_pearl: A normal EF is not an electrical clearance test.

evidence.claim: Arrhythmia surveillance is part of myocarditis follow-up and return-to-activity assessment.
Persistent arrhythmic risk can remain after the acute inflammatory phase.

questions.concept: electrical risk independent of troponin trend
questions.learning_objective: Avoid using a falling troponin to de-escalate monitoring when conduction disease or arrhythmia persists.
questions.stem: A 12-year-old with myocarditis has a falling troponin concentration but intermittent second-degree/high-grade AV block continues on telemetry. What is the best management implication?

options.text: Continue monitored care because biomarker improvement does not establish electrical recovery
Discharge because falling troponin proves the myocardium is electrically stable
Stop telemetry to avoid overdiagnosing transient conduction findings
Begin graded sports participation to test the conduction system
Treat only symptoms and ignore asymptomatic high-grade conduction abnormalities

questions.rationale: Biomarkers and conduction-system recovery can follow different timelines. Persistent high-grade block remains a high-risk electrical finding even if the injury marker is improving.

option_explanations.continue_monitor: Correct. The active management problem is now electrical stability, not simply biomarker direction.
option_explanations.discharge_troponin: Troponin decline is encouraging but cannot substitute for rhythm stability and adequate perfusion.
option_explanations.stop_telemetry: Telemetry is precisely how intermittent conduction disease is recognized; stopping it would discard clinically relevant information.
option_explanations.sports: Exercise is restricted during active/recent myocarditis and is not a diagnostic stress test for unstable conduction disease.
option_explanations.ignore_block: High-grade AV block can deteriorate even when symptoms are intermittent; it warrants specialist evaluation and monitored care.

questions.board_pearl: Do not let a better laboratory trend cancel an abnormal rhythm strip.

evidence.claim: Pediatric myocarditis with heart block warrants high-acuity monitoring and therapy.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize polymorphic ventricular tachycardia as an immediate life-threatening complication even when EF is preserved.
questions.stem: A 14-year-old with myocarditis has preserved LV systolic function but develops palpitations, near-syncope, and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia on telemetry. Which interpretation is most important?

options.text: This is potentially life-threatening electrical instability requiring urgent escalation regardless of preserved EF
Preserved EF makes the rhythm low risk
The rhythm proves isolated pericarditis
The rhythm indicates that myocarditis has resolved
Outpatient rhythm follow-up is sufficient because the child still has a pulse

questions.rationale: Malignant ventricular arrhythmia can occur without severe global pump dysfunction. The immediate risk is electrical, and preserved EF does not protect against deterioration to cardiac arrest.

option_explanations.life_threatening: Correct. Near-syncope plus polymorphic VT is an acute escalation trigger.
option_explanations.benign_ef: EF measures global systolic performance and cannot exclude a dangerous arrhythmogenic substrate.
option_explanations.pericarditis: Polymorphic VT signifies myocardial electrical involvement, not isolated pericardial inflammation.
option_explanations.resolved: A new malignant arrhythmia is evidence of ongoing risk, not resolution.
option_explanations.outpatient: A pulse does not make a malignant rhythm safe for outpatient management, especially with near-syncope.

questions.board_pearl: Myocarditis can be electrically malignant even when the echocardiogram looks mechanically reassuring.

evidence.claim: Ventricular arrhythmias are major high-risk complications of pediatric myocarditis.
Arrhythmias in pediatric myocarditis are associated with increased morbidity/resource utilization.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize recurrent ventricular arrhythmia plus low-output physiology as a trigger for advanced-center/MCS escalation rather than treating rhythm and circulation as separate problems.
questions.stem: A 9-year-old with myocarditis has recurrent ventricular tachycardia despite initial rhythm treatment. Between episodes, ventricular function is severely depressed, lactate is rising, urine output is falling, and vasoactive needs are increasing. Which strategic response is best?

options.text: Treat the child as having combined electrical and pump instability and activate advanced heart-failure/MCS-level escalation now
Focus only on suppressing the arrhythmia because circulation will recover once the rhythm is controlled
Ignore the ventricular tachycardia and treat only ejection fraction
Delay MCS-center involvement until cardiac arrest occurs
Suspend escalation until a viral or biopsy diagnosis is finalized

questions.rationale: Recurrent malignant arrhythmia plus refractory low output is a high-risk pre-arrest myocarditis phenotype. Rhythm management, perfusion support, and advanced-center/MCS planning must occur in parallel.

option_explanations.combined_escalation: Correct. Electrical and mechanical instability amplify each other and should be managed as one deteriorating syndrome.
option_explanations.rhythm_only: Termination of VT may improve output, but severe underlying pump failure and organ hypoperfusion remain independent threats.
option_explanations.pump_only: Ventricular tachycardia can itself cause arrest and worsen output; it cannot be ignored because EF is severely depressed.
option_explanations.wait_arrest: Current pediatric guidance favors early transfer/MCS consideration before arrest in refractory low output.
option_explanations.etiology_delay: Etiologic clarification may affect disease-specific therapy but should not delay stabilization or advanced-support planning.

questions.board_pearl: When myocarditis is both electrically and mechanically unstable, escalation must address both domains simultaneously.

evidence.claim: Pediatric myocarditis with arrhythmia and refractory low cardiac output is a pre-arrest state in which early ICU and MCS-capable-center escalation is recommended/reasonable.
Fulminant myocarditis may require early mechanical circulatory support to prevent irreversible organ injury.
